summary.text: 少 commonly means “few” or “less.” One proposed reading of its early strokes is grains gathered in a small amount, but what they depict is uncertain; early spellings used for 少 and 小 overlap for “few” and “small.”

formation.text: A proposed pictographic analysis sees grains, perhaps sand, in the early graph and connects their small quantity with “few.” The referent and original construction remain uncertain. The received Shuowen account instead parses 少 as 小, meaning “small,” plus 丿 as a phonetic element; this is a historical analysis, not settled proof of the graph’s original design.

components.text: The received Shuowen analysis assigns 小 the meaning “small” in 少. Early 少 and 小 spellings overlap in form and use, so this later parsing does not prove that 小 was a separate part of the original graph.
The received Shuowen analysis assigns 丿 a phonetic role in 少. That historical parsing does not establish that the stroke belonged to the graph’s original design.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin reading pair does not establish the ancient sound relation proposed in the received Shuowen analysis.

sound.text: In modern Mandarin, 丿 is piě and 少 is shǎo; this present-day comparison does not confirm their proposed historical relation.

history.text: Early forms conventionally transcribed as 少 or 小 overlap in shape and use. Bronze forms are described with a slanting stroke that distinguishes 少 from 小, but the point when their uses became consistently distinct is uncertain. The curated oracle-style image is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph, and does not establish what the strokes depict.

The received Shuowen explanation glosses 少 as “not many” and parses it as 小 plus phonetic 丿. Historical sound-series analyses disagree over whether 少 and 小 were related in pronunciation; reconstructions of 少 alone do not resolve that question.

uncertainties.text: The early strokes’ referent—grains of sand, rice, or something else—and whether “small” or “few” was the graph’s original meaning remain unresolved. The grain picture is a proposal.
The available evidence does not establish a dated path connecting “small,” “few,” “young,” “insufficient,” and “short time.”

senses.period: Oracle-bone and bronze inscription usage reported; precise earliest date unresolved
senses.text: Early spellings transcribed as 少 or 小 are reported for “few”; bronze examples include use in contrast with 多. Their priority relative to “small” is not established.

senses.text: Early spellings transcribed as 少 or 小 are also reported for “small.” Their overlap does not establish which meaning came first.

senses.text: Bronze examples and historical dictionary entries record “young” or “youthful”; how this sense developed is not established.
Historical dictionary entries record “short time”; its emergence and relation to the other meanings are unresolved.
Historical dictionary entries record “insufficient” or “lacking”; their development from another sense is not established.

limitations.text: No precise earliest dated attestation or complete dated sequence of meanings is established. Early uses for “small” and “few” do not prove a developmental link; dictionary ordering is not chronology.

overview.text: 少 commonly means “few” or “less.” One proposal reads its early strokes as grains—perhaps sand—shown in a small amount, but the referent is uncertain.

components.text: The received Shuowen parsing gives 小 the idea “small”; early overlap means this need not reflect a separate original part.
The received Shuowen parsing assigns 丿 a sound role, though its place in the original graph is uncertain.

relationships.text: The received Shuowen analysis assigns 小 a semantic role in 少, while competing accounts treat early 少 and 小 as overlapping forms that may not have had this separate component structure.
The received Shuowen analysis assigns 丿 a phonetic role in 少. The modern Mandarin pair piě–shǎo does not establish that historical relation or confirm the original design.
